channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: AI-related computing infrastructure investment reached about 1.4% of US GDP in the first quarter of 2026, up from 0.7% a year earlier, and is described by Epoch AI as the largest driver of growth in US private investment.
item.description:
The St. Louis Fed found that information-processing equipment accounted for 39% of total GDP growth through the third quarter of 2025, a larger share than during the dot-com boom. The political dimension cuts against the economics: a CNN analysis found opposition to data centres is bipartisan because the disputes are local, which means they do not follow national party lines. This sits directly alongside the Associated General Contractors' July construction spending figures, where data centres, highways and power projects were named as the categories propping up a total that fell 3.8% year-on-year.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Data centre and AI infrastructure build-out uses a materially different set of adhesive technologies from commercial or residential building: thermal interface materials, electronics assembly adhesives, structural bonding and sealing for equipment enclosures, rather than flooring, glazing and general fit-out systems. So a US construction market where the total is falling while highways, data centres and power projects hold it up is one where the product mix may shift even if volumes hold. The bipartisan local opposition is the risk to that: an investment concentrated in a category facing site-by-site permitting resistance carries a different kind of uncertainty from a cyclical one. Points that may be worth considering include whether the data-centre product range is positioned to absorb the share shift the construction data implies, and how permitting resistance is factored into US demand scenarios.

Fortune | Associated General Contractors of America

item.title: The UN Environment Programme's Limit Overshoot report says global warming is likely to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels within the next few years, peaking at about 1.8°C even if national plans are fully implemented.
item.description:
The two accounts of the report differ on the upper end. One puts warming at roughly 2.6°C under current policies; the other says peaks up to 2°C are expected in scenarios other than the most optimistic. Both give 1.8°C as the best case; one adds that the threshold crossed is the limit set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, and describes the crossing as likely rather than certain. The report frames this as an overshoot rather than a permanent failure, setting out a three-step path of exceeding the threshold, reaching a peak and then reducing, with the last step requiring large-scale intervention. Long-term warming is put at about 1.4°C at present, with occasional short-term spikes above that.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Formal acknowledgement that the Paris threshold will be crossed tends to precede regulatory tightening rather than relaxation, because an overshoot framing puts the emphasis on the speed of reduction after the peak. For chemical manufacturers that bears on the direction of carbon pricing, product-level emissions disclosure and the compostability rules already appearing in packaging law. The physical side bears on logistics and feedstock availability rather than on compliance. Points that may be worth considering include whether internal carbon price assumptions are set against a 1.5°C or a 1.8°C-plus trajectory.

Bloomberg | Il Sole 24 Ore

item.title: The Taiwan Ceramic Industry Association's chairman has called for a border carbon tax on imported ceramic goods and anti-dumping duties on tiles from Southeast Asia and India, in an industry that has fallen from 128 tile companies at its peak to 19.
item.description:
The call was made by the association's chairman, Lin Yòu-yǔ, rather than by government, and no official response is reported. Reporting notes a long contraction: tile producers down from 128 at the industry's peak to 19, and production kilns from 260 to 57. Two instruments are being sought at once and they work differently — a border carbon adjustment prices the embedded emissions of imports, while anti-dumping duties address below-cost pricing from named origins — which suggests the association sees both a cost-of-carbon disadvantage and a pricing problem. It follows South Korea's decision on 1 September to impose anti-dumping duties on Chinese butyl acrylate — a decided government measure, unlike this association request.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Tile is an adhesive technologies application: tile adhesives, grouts and levelling compounds follow ceramic volumes, so where tiles are produced and consumed matters more than the trade instrument itself. If duties were imposed, the effect on installation-materials demand in Taiwan would be limited, since tiles would still be laid whatever their origin, but the location of tile manufacturing could shift, which would affect demand for the materials used in production rather than installation. The broader pattern: a Taiwanese industry association is now requesting a border carbon adjustment, an instrument so far associated with the EU. Points that may be worth considering include how many Asian markets could plausibly adopt carbon border measures on construction materials, and what that would mean for the embedded-emissions data customers ask suppliers to provide.

Commercial Times

item.title: New orders at US factories rose 0.9% in July to USD 663.6 billion, above the 0.6% economists expected and snapping a two-month losing streak, though the increase leaned heavily on a 12.7% rise in orders for civilian aircraft and parts.
item.description:
The composition tempers the headline. Excluding the aircraft category, the picture is flatter: motor vehicle bodies, parts and trailers rose 0.4% and machinery 0.8%, while computers and electronic products fell 1.1% — though that category is 14.3% higher than a year earlier — and electrical equipment, appliances and components fell 0.3%. The Federal Reserve's Beige Book, published in the same period, described overall activity as increasing modestly since early July, with consumer spending up slightly, consumers highly price-sensitive because of inflation, and demand for high-priced goods nonetheless holding up. It also recorded household and business confidence under pressure from policy questions, high energy prices and uncertainty around the Iran war, while describing the overall outlook as positive. August ISM readings were mixed: the index fell a point to 54.6 but stayed in expansion, with new orders at their lowest since March and factory employment up for a second month at a slower pace, while the production sub-index reached its second-highest level since the end of 2021.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A rebound concentrated in civilian aircraft is a narrow one, and the categories closest to adhesive technologies demand moved little: motor vehicle parts up 0.4%, machinery up 0.8%, electrical equipment and appliances down 0.3%. Read alongside the ISM new-orders reading at a five-month low, the picture is of US manufacturing holding roughly flat rather than accelerating, with a 12.7% rise in the civilian aircraft and parts category flattering the monthly total. The Beige Book's observation that consumers are highly price-sensitive while high-priced goods still sell is a useful distinction for judging where pass-through is achievable. Points that may be worth considering include whether US order-book assumptions rest on the headline series or on the categories that map to actual product demand.

MarketScreener | The Economic Times | Commercial Times | Yahoo Taiwan

item.title: The German cabinet approved a draft income tax reform worth about EUR 10 billion a year from 2028, and the DIW raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.2% from 0.5%, citing stronger exports and a milder energy shock than feared.
item.description:
The two-stage reform is to take effect on 1 January 2027. The basic tax-free allowance rises from EUR 12,348 this year to EUR 12,564 next year and EUR 12,900 in 2028; the 42% top rate applies later, from EUR 70,600 rather than EUR 69,879, flattening the tariff between roughly EUR 17,800 and EUR 70,600; child benefit rises from EUR 259 to EUR 267 and then EUR 272; the employee deduction rises from EUR 1,230 to EUR 1,430; and the tax-free ceiling for Sunday and holiday premium hourly wages rises from EUR 50 to EUR 75. Financing comes from higher earners: the 45% rate on incomes above EUR 250,000, and a new 47% rate above EUR 280,000. Klingbeil's proposals to fund further relief through higher inheritance tax and a higher top rate were rejected by the coalition partner. The DIW forecast is 1.2% for 2026, 1.0% for 2027 and 0.7% for 2028, and carries an important qualification: about 70% of this year's growth is attributed to public consumption and investment, so the private-sector contribution remains small. Separate reporting notes German output grew 0.2% last year after contracting in 2023 and 2024, and identifies Chinese competition in the same product categories as a structural reason for the stagnation.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

A growth upgrade driven roughly 70% by public spending describes a different demand environment from one driven by private investment, and the relevant question for suppliers is which categories the public component reaches, which the DIW release does not break down. The tax reform is a 2027 and 2028 effect on household income rather than a near-term demand change, and the described relief of more than EUR 600 a year for families with children is modest against consumer-goods volumes. The forecast path declines from 1.2% to 1.0% to 0.7%, even though the institute presents the revision as a turning point. Points that may be worth considering include whether German demand planning distinguishes publicly funded from privately funded activity, and how the 2028 profile is reflected in medium-term capacity decisions.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Fortune | AP

item.title: Xi Jinping and Abdel Fattah el-Sisi agreed to expand Chinese investment in the Suez Canal Economic Zone and launch a third phase of the Egyptian-Chinese industrial zone, which officials say hosts 200 companies and about USD 4 billion.
item.description:
Egypt has not announced a figure for the new investment. The two presidents signed a joint statement on deepening their comprehensive strategic partnership, alongside multiple cooperation agreements marking the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations that covered Belt and Road cooperation, artificial intelligence, trade, and industry and supply-chain partnerships. The joint statement names renewable energy, data centres, semiconductors, space applications, critical-mineral supply chains, agriculture and car manufacturing as areas to explore, and the two sides welcomed renewing and possibly expanding their currency-swap arrangement, calling for greater use of the yuan and the Egyptian pound in trade settlement. Xi used the visit — his first to the Middle East in four years — to call on regional states to oppose external interference and consider reshaping the region's security order, and said China is ready to work with them to safeguard shipping routes, an issue reporting links to disruption through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb. Chinese customs data put China's trade surplus with Egypt at USD 12 billion in the first seven months of 2026. Separately, China's zero-tariff policy for imports from 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations is expected to support Egyptian agricultural exports.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The Suez Canal Economic Zone is a manufacturing location as well as a transit point, and a third phase of an industrial zone already holding 200 companies represents additional production capacity positioned at the entrance to the European market. That is relevant both as a possible supply base and as a source of competing product. The currency-swap and settlement language would give bilateral trade a non-dollar settlement option, though the sources describe an expansion of local-currency use rather than a replacement of dollar clearing. Points that may be worth considering include whether the Suez zone features in current European supply-base scenarios, and how settlement-currency flexibility is handled where counterparties in the region shift toward yuan.

The Africa Report | South China Morning Post | The Standard | Dawn | MarketScreener | China Daily | Chinatimes | China Daily

item.title: Standard Chartered raised its 2026 Taiwan growth forecast to 11.5% from 9.5%, which would be the fastest since 2010, while Singapore's consensus forecast rose to 5.0% from 3.5% and a Thai business group lifted its range to 2.1–2.5% from 1.6–2.0%.
item.description:
Taiwan's official statistics office puts 2026 growth at 11.05%, so the two estimates differ and both are worth carrying. Standard Chartered also raised its 2027 forecast to 6.5% from 5%, holding inflation forecasts at 2.1% and 2%. Its reasoning is that AI demand continues to drive exports and technology investment and is spreading into private consumption: in the second quarter, domestic demand contributed 7.3 percentage points against net exports at 5.6, with fixed investment adding 3.1 and private consumption 2.6. Taiwan's business cycle monitor has flashed red for eight consecutive months and listed and over-the-counter company revenue rose 33.7% in the seven months to July. In Singapore, the Monetary Authority's survey of economists raised 2026 growth to 5.0% after the second quarter came in at 5.9% against a 4.3% forecast, with manufacturing — about 20% of GDP — now expected to grow 8.4%. Thailand's Joint Standing Committee on Commerce, Industry and Banking raised its range on stronger exports and private investment, lifting its export forecast to 12–16% from 8–10%, but warned that the benefits are increasingly uneven: transmission into the domestic economy has weakened, production leans heavily on imported components, and new projects are creating fewer jobs than comparable past cycles.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The AI and semiconductor cycle drives the Taiwan and Singapore upgrades, while Thailand's rests on exports and private investment more broadly, so this is a concentrated rather than a uniform Asian expansion. For adhesive technologies the relevant exposure is electronics assembly materials, where Taiwan and Singapore sit at the centre of the demand, rather than the general industrial or construction ranges. The Thai caution is the useful counterweight: a headline upgrade built on exports with high imported content and weak domestic transmission does not necessarily translate into local demand growth. Taiwan's own numbers carry a similar caveat, since the business-cycle signal and the revenue growth are both concentrated in semiconductors and high-performance computing. Points that may be worth considering include whether Asian demand assumptions distinguish electronics-linked volumes from general industrial ones, and how durable a forecast resting on one technology cycle is judged to be.

Commercial Times | Chinatimes | Commercial Times | MarketScreener | Channel News Asia | Bangkok Post | The Nation

item.title: Bank of Japan governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank will debate raising rates at its 17–18 September meeting, focusing on whether inflation risks are intensifying, while the ECB's Joachim Nagel signalled support for a further increase on 10 September.
item.description:
Ueda said policymakers will assess whether conditions are developing in line with projections and whether upside price risks are building, and noted core inflation approaching 2%; board member Hajime Takata has called for flexible rate adjustments. Totan Research puts the probability of a move from 1% to 1.25% at the September meeting above 90%, though that is one research house's estimate. Nagel, who also heads the Bundesbank, told Le Monde that financial markets correctly understand how the ECB is likely to respond on 10 September; the Council is widely expected to raise the deposit facility rate by 25 basis points to 2.50%, following a quarter-point increase in June. Accounts of the US position differ in tone. The Treasury readout after Bessent met Ueda has him calling for monetary policy that avoids excess exchange-rate volatility and supporting the steps Japan has already taken on what he called significant yen undervaluation, pointing to yen weakness as a contributor to Japanese inflation; other reporting has him urging Japan to take decisive monetary measures. Bond markets have moved ahead of all of this. The Bloomberg Global Government Bond Index yield rose for a fourth consecutive session to 3.72%, reported as the highest since mid-2008, with the UK 30-year at 5.88% (highest since 1998), Germany's 10-year at 3.339% (highest since 2011), Japan's 30-year above 4.18% and the US 10-year at 4.77% to 4.78% after an intraday 4.798%.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Two of the three major central banks now have meetings within eight days at which a rise is the expected outcome, which means the cost of capital is likely to reset in Europe and Japan almost simultaneously rather than in sequence. The global index reading matters more than any single market: a yield level last seen in mid-2008, described by some commentators as a systematic repricing rather than a local move, changes the discount rate applied to long-dated industrial investment everywhere at once. German 10-year yields at their highest since 2011 are the most direct read for European capital planning. Points that may be worth considering include whether projects with European financing dates in the fourth quarter are tested against a further 25 basis points, and how a simultaneous European and Japanese move would interact with existing currency assumptions.

The Economic Times | Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Anadolu Agency | The Mainichi | Hong Kong Commercial Daily | Business Day

item.title: Canada's counter-tariffs on more than CAD 27 billion of US-made products take effect on 8 September and cover joinery, vinyl flooring, lighting, plastics, wooden kitchen furniture and appliances, alongside a 50% duty on US motorcycles above 800cc.
item.description:
The list is weighted toward construction and interior fit-out. Kelly Rogers of the Canadian Home Builders' Association in Newfoundland and Labrador said the duties add to an already difficult period for construction, which faces a skilled-labour shortage, new regulations, a new national building code and rising material costs. The motorcycle duty applies to US-origin internal-combustion machines above 800cc; it does not name Harley-Davidson, though reporting expects it to cover many US-built Harley models. The two sides' measures are of a similar order but cover opposite flows: the Canadian counter-tariff list is put at over CAD 27 billion of US-made goods, while Prime Minister Carney is reported as saying US levies affect about CAD 29 billion of Canadian goods. Politically, positions are hardening on both sides. Republican members of Congress publicly backed the president and blamed Ottawa for leaving negotiations, while US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer was pressed at a Republican Study Committee lunch by House Republicans, particularly members from northern border states, about the harm a trade war could do to their local economies. A practical example surfaced in Manitoba, where the province's utility may not proceed with buying three GE Vernova gas turbines for a CAD 3 billion generating station expansion.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The product list is the operative detail. Vinyl flooring, plastics, joinery and wooden kitchen furniture are categories where adhesive technologies are embedded in the product rather than in its transport, so a duty on the finished goods reaches suppliers through their customers' Canadian volumes rather than through any direct exposure. The Newfoundland and Labrador homebuilders' association comment locates the pressure in residential construction, a different demand channel from the highway, data-centre and power categories propping up the US total. The Manitoba turbine case illustrates a second-order effect worth noting: procurement decisions being reconsidered because of the dispute rather than because of the tariff arithmetic. Points that may be worth considering include which North American customer volumes run through the named product categories, and whether Canadian fit-out demand is modelled separately from new-build.

CBC | Yahoo Canada | Yahoo Canada | POLITICO | CBC | CBC

item.title: An Italian decree-law makes compostability mandatory for selected packaging formats used for fresh fruit and vegetables, food service and catering, single portions and hospitality, under a flexibility the EU packaging regulation allows.
item.description:
Italy has invoked Article 9(2)(b) of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, which allows a member state to require additional packaging formats to be compostable where effective biowaste collection and organic recycling systems are in place. European Bioplastics, the trade association for the sector, welcomed the decree and framed the effect as allowing the selected applications to continue being designed for organic recycling, provided they are certified compostable and correctly handled at end of life. The reporting available comes from the association rather than from the Italian government, and does not state the date the requirements take effect or the compliance deadlines. What it does establish is the mechanism: the PPWR sets a European floor, and individual member states can go further for named formats where their waste infrastructure supports it, which means packaging rules for the same product can now differ between EU markets by design rather than by transposition delay.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Compostability is a whole-package property, so it reaches adhesives directly: a laminate, label or closure that is not itself certified compostable can disqualify an otherwise compliant pack. The formats named — fresh produce trays and films, food service and catering, single portions, hospitality — are ones where bonded and laminated structures are common. The more consequential point may be the precedent rather than the Italian market: if other member states with mature biowaste collection use the same Article 9(2)(b) flexibility, converters will face a patchwork of national compostability mandates within the single market, and product ranges may need country-specific specifications. Points that may be worth considering include which adhesive systems in food-contact and food-service applications hold current compostability certification, and whether the Italian formats are supplied from a single European specification today.

European Bioplastics | European Bioplastics

item.title: Reporting citing finance minister Lars Klingbeil says Berlin will finalise a package on Chinese trade practices within weeks; options include joint ventures for Chinese entrants, tariffs on hybrid cars, and "Buy European" procurement.
item.description:
The measures described are options rather than decisions, and no timetable beyond "the coming weeks" is given. Klingbeil is reported as saying German manufacturers are becoming more cautious about China, which he says encourages the government to take a tougher line. Chinese state media carried the reporting alongside expert commentary arguing the package would backfire. In parallel, the European Commission is in talks with Beijing on reducing the EU's trade deficit with China, running at about EUR 1 billion a day, and is expected to present results at the EU summit in mid-October; the EU's view is that Chinese export subsidies are pushing many European industrial sectors out of the market. The Industrial Accelerator Act, which would limit Chinese investment in strategic sectors including solar panels, raw materials and electric vehicles and set Made-in-EU public procurement requirements, drew support from industry representatives at a European Parliament hearing, where participants warned that time is running out to curb Chinese exports. The draft's origin rules are strict — for electric vehicles under supported programmes, assembly in the EU and at least 70% European content by value excluding the battery — and Swiss suppliers may be caught by them, since it is not yet settled whether Swiss companies count as European. The EU is separately backing a new generation of battery manufacturers with billions of euros to reduce dependence on China.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Local-content rules are the part of the package that reaches suppliers rather than only importers. A 70% European-content threshold excluding the battery, applied to publicly supported vehicle programmes, would make the origin of the adhesive technologies used in assembly a qualifying question rather than a commercial one, and the unresolved Swiss position shows the definition of "European" is still being drawn. Joint-venture requirements for Chinese entrants would change the ownership structure of potential customers in Europe rather than their number. Set against the tightening, the battery funding programme creates a new European customer base in cell manufacturing. Points that may be worth considering include whether supply into EU vehicle programmes could evidence European origin at a 70% threshold, and how the Swiss question is being tracked given its bearing on non-EU European plants.

Chinatimes | Global Times | Politico Europe | Politico Europe | Neue Zürcher Zeitung | Deutsche Welle

item.title: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said preparations are under way to sanction 1,600 more individuals and companies tied to Russia's military-industrial complex, after the attempted explosive-drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport in early August.
item.description:
The scale is the notable part. Reporting notes that previous packages carried 100 to 200 listings each, totalling close to 3,000 over four and a half years; this one would add 1,600 at once, aimed principally at Russian arms companies and their suppliers. For many of those companies the change is qualitative: they were already barred from receiving war-relevant goods from the EU, and the intention now is to prohibit all business activity with them. Kallas said more listings may be added. Reporting describes the Leipzig incident as bearing the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism. Germany says it has evidence of Russian involvement in the 4 August attack, and has announced its own measures: closing the Russian Consulate General in Bonn from 18 September, terminating the contract with the Russian House in Berlin, and increasing pressure on the shadow fleet. Investigators have reportedly identified two suspects, described as a Russian national holding a Latvian passport and a man from Belarus holding a Russian passport. Moscow rejects the account: Putin accused Berlin of fabricating evidence to distract from domestic difficulties, and Deputy Security Council chairman Dmitry Medvedev threatened retaliation against Germany, referring to defence companies working for Ukraine and "quite a few other places in Berlin". Separately, two further attacks on the German power grid, in southern Brandenburg and near Cologne, prompted the utilities association BDEW to call on the federal and state governments for an immediate package on drone detection and large-scale no-fly zones over critical infrastructure under the planned U-Space Act.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Two distinct exposures sit in this story. The sanctions change is a compliance one: moving hundreds of entities from a goods-specific prohibition to a full business ban widens the screening question from what is being supplied to whether any relationship exists at all, and 1,600 listings arriving together is a larger single update than counterparty systems have had to absorb in this conflict. The second is physical. Attacks on electricity infrastructure and on Leipzig/Halle airport, and an industry association publicly saying the state has not resolved who protects what, bear on operating continuity for energy-intensive manufacturing rather than on trade compliance. Points that may be worth considering include how quickly a 1,600-name update can be run through supplier and customer screening, and whether site-level continuity planning in Germany currently assumes grid interruption as a security rather than a weather event.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Il Sole 24 Ore | Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung
